node.label: Donald Worster
node.date_label: Nature's Economy 1977 · Dust Bowl 1979 · Rivers of Empire 1985 · 'Transformations of the Earth' 1990 · coverage through 2000
node.description: A historian of the American Great Plains and arid West who set out a three-level model of environmental history. In 'Doing Environmental History' (1988) he wrote that 'there are three levels on which the new history proceeds': 'understanding nature itself', 'the socioeconomic realm as it interacts with the environment', and 'the purely mental or intellectual', which together 'constitute a single dynamic inquiry'. His 1990 Journal of American History essay turned to 'that middle level, the analysis of modes of production as ecological phenomena', chiefly the capitalist transformation of agriculture, which Dust Bowl (1979) had called 'the decisive factor in this nation's use of nature'; Rivers of Empire (1985) described the West as 'a modern hydraulic society'. Merchant's 1990 response called the levels 'a significant framework for research and writing in this emerging field' but found that the essay 'lacks a gender analysis'. Cronon (1992) read Dust Bowl as a story whose 'chief agent' is capitalism and whose plot 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy'.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Donald Worster (b. 1941); Nature's Economy: The Roots of Ecology (1977); Dust Bowl: The Southern Plains in the 1930s (1979); Rivers of Empire: Water, Aridity, and the Growth of the American West (1985); 'Appendix: Doing Environmental History', in The Ends of the Earth (1988); 'Transformations of the Earth: Toward an Agroecological Perspective in History', Journal of American History (1990), reprinted in The Wealth of Nature (1993). Readings: Merchant's round-table response (1990); Cronon, 'A Place for Stories' (1992); Hennessey's review of Rivers of Empire (1987); McDean (1986).
node.scope_note: This entry presents the three-level model in Worster's 1988 wording, checked in an abridged reprint and by full-text search of the 1988 edition, and the 1990 essay in his own 1993 reprint; the Journal of American History pages of 1990 were not reachable and are given only where another writer cites them (Isenberg 2013). Dust Bowl and Rivers of Empire are quoted at the pages given by Cronon (1992) and Hennessey (1987), with the wording confirmed by search of the original editions. He is not presented as the founder of the field or the sole author of the scheme: he grounds the idea in Aldo Leopold's call for 'an ecological interpretation of history', and Arthur McEvoy's ecology, production and cognition triad appeared in the same 1988 volume. The scheme was contested at once: Merchant (1990) added gender and 'a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction', Cronon (1992) treated Dust Bowl as a declensionist narrative, and McDean (1986) criticised its generalisation across the Plains. The 1990 objections of White and Cronon in the round table are known here only through Isenberg (2013), a later reading.

proposed_edges.relationship: Three levels of environmental history (nature, modes of production, ideas), with the capitalist transformation of agriculture as the middle level (1979–1990)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Worster's own statements, in-period first. 'Appendix: Doing Environmental History', The Ends of the Earth (1988), read in an abridged reprint and checked by full-text search of the 1988 edition, whose running heads place the passage between pp. 292 and 294 (Isenberg 2013 cites p. 293): 'There are three levels on which the new history proceeds, three clusters of issues it addresses'; 'The first deals with understanding nature itself, as organized and functioning in past times'; 'The second level in this history brings in the socioeconomic realm as it interacts with the environment. Here we are concerned with tools and work, with the social relations that grow out of that work, with the various modes people have devised of producing goods from natural resources'; the third is 'the purely mental or intellectual, in which perceptions, ethics, laws, myths, and other structures of meaning become part of an individual's or group's dialogue with nature'; together they 'constitute a single dynamic inquiry'. 'Transformations of the Earth' (JAH 1990; English text checked in Worster's 1993 reprint in The Wealth of Nature, ch. 4; JAH page as cited by Isenberg): 'most environmental historians seem to have settled philosophically on a position that is at once materialist and idealist', yet the essay turns to 'that middle level, the analysis of modes of production as ecological phenomena' (p. 1091), and proposes that 'the single most important task for scholars in the history of modern agroecology is to trace what Karl Polanyi has called “the great transformation”'. Dust Bowl (1979) had argued: 'Capitalism, it is my contention, has been the decisive factor in this nation's use of nature' (p. 5, as quoted by Cronon 1992, p. 1363; wording confirmed in the 1979 edition). In-period readings: Merchant's 1990 response (read) calls his 'conceptual levels of ecology (natural history), production (technology and its socioeconomic relations), and cognition' 'a significant framework for research and writing in this emerging field', while the essay 'lacks a gender analysis' and environmental history 'needs a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction' (p. 1117). Cronon (1992, read) finds that in Dust Bowl 'the chief agent of the story is not “the pioneers” or “civilization” or “man”; it is capitalism', a plot that 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy' (p. 1363). McDean (1986) criticises the generalisation across the Plains (existing source, not re-read). A contribution, not a founding: Worster takes the idea from Aldo Leopold, who 'spoke of “an ecological interpretation of history”' (1988), and McEvoy's ecology, production and cognition triad appeared in the same 1988 volume. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: Isenberg (2013, pp. 88–89) reports White's and Cronon's 1990 objections ('superstructure in the old vulgar Marxist sense'; 'potentially excessive materialism'), whose texts are unread here; McNeill (2003, p. 37) writes of environmental historians' theories that 'The most cogent was probably the one elaborated in slightly different versions by both Donald Worster and Arthur McEvoy', but that such theories 'have sparked no groundswells of enthusiasm'.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: agriculture_capitalism ('Agricultural capitalism and environmental crisis'; Worster alone; Dust Bowl and 'The Dirty Thirties') matches the 1990 essay's middle level and the Dust Bowl thesis. No environment strand states the three-level model itself; a reviewer could add one at release (for example 'Three levels of environmental history: nature, production, cognition', holding Worster with Merchant's fourth level and McEvoy). dust_causal_debate and malin_adaptation_debate are disputes over the 1930s Plains and rest on the 1986 exchange, not on the framework.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: The capitalism argument (Dust Bowl, p. 5; the 1990 'great transformation' via Polanyi) is an environmental historian's use of political economy. No checked text shows economic historians taking it up as a contribution to their field; the one economist's review found (Rucker, Journal of Economic History 1986, on Rivers of Empire) is paywalled and unread. edge_267 (economic — environment, comparison) already names 'Worster's agriculture'. Not proposed.

Rivers of Empire (1985) calls the West 'a modern hydraulic society' and, in Hennessey's 1987 review (read), describes 'a social order based on the intensive, large-scale manipulation of water' (p. 7) and the gap 'between what irrigation technology promised and what it delivered'. Hennessey calls it 'a social historical analysis of irrigation' and says it 'focuses primarily on the ideas behind irrigation'. The argument is about power and the state (Wittfogel revised), and no checked text places it in the history of technology. The technology entry has no water or irrigation strand. Not proposed.

Nature's Economy (1977) is a history of ecological ideas, built on an 'arcadian' stance (Gilbert White) and an 'imperial' tradition (Linnaeus); the book's own index gives the imperial tradition at pp. 2, 29–55. Merchant (1990, p. 1117) credits 'his account of the changing history of ecological ideas in his major books', and Cronon (1993, p. 3, as recorded in canon-evidence-international.md; it is the Cronon packet's pe131_cronon_uses_1993) says Merchant 'joined Worster in bringing an environmentalist perspective to the history of science'. The book itself was checked only by search snippets, Worster has no science roster row, and no science strand covers the history of ecology. Possible later edge; not proposed now.

Worster's 1990 note 5 names Braudel, Febvre and Le Roy Ladurie as 'Another important source of ideas' for the field (see NOTES.md, 'Annales passage (for edge_111)'). That is his report of the field's sources, not a contribution by Worster to Annales history. It is evidence for the planned revision of edge_111, not for a person edge.

He is in the geography strand hewes_farming_resource because 'The Dirty Thirties' (1986) uses Hewes's suitcase-farming study. Use of a geographer's work is not a contribution to geography, and he has no geography roster row. Not proposed.

new_sources.title: Donald Worster, “Appendix: Doing Environmental History,” in Donald Worster, ed., The Ends of the Earth: Perspectives on Modern Environmental History (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1988), 289–307.
new_sources.citation: Donald Worster, “Appendix: Doing Environmental History,” in Worster, ed., The Ends of the Earth: Perspectives on Modern Environmental History (Cambridge University Press, 1988), 289–307.

verification.note: Read in the abridged reprint in Carolyn Merchant, ed., Major Problems in American Environmental History (Cengage, 3rd ed.), ch. 1, reader pp. 2–9, which omits passages with ellipses; the reader's pagination is not the original's. The 1988 edition (Internet Archive endsofearthpersp0000unse, lending-restricted, page images not seen) was checked by the archive's full-text search: the contents list the appendix at p. 289; running heads '290', '292' and '294 Appendix: Doing Environmental History' fall before 'through time and, conversely', 'remain spontaneous and self-generating' and 'grazed and chopped out, bluegrass' respectively, so the three-level passage lies between pp. 292 and 294 (Isenberg 2013, n. 19, cites p. 293). Search confirmed the 1988 wording of 'three levels on which the new history proceeds, three clusters of issues', 'understanding nature itself, as organized and functioning in', 'The second level in this history brings in the socioeconomic realm as it interacts with the environment', 'forming a third level for the historian is that more intangible and uniquely', 'the purely mental or intellectual, in which perceptions, ethics', 'constitute a single dynamic inquiry in which nature, social and economic', 'born out of a moral purpose, with strong political commitments', and Leopold's 'ecological interpretation of history'. Isenberg 2013 quotes the second level as 'as it interacts with nature'; the 1988 text reads 'with the environment'. The book index gives modes of production at pp. 298–302 (the section 'Human Modes of Production'). Exact page breaks inside pp. 292–294 were not seen.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period: Worster's statement of the three-level model.

new_sources.title: Donald Worster, “Transformations of the Earth: Toward an Agroecological Perspective in History,” Journal of American History 76, no. 4 (March 1990): 1087–1106.
new_sources.citation: Donald Worster, “Transformations of the Earth: Toward an Agroecological Perspective in History,” Journal of American History 76:4 (1990): 1087–1106, opening “A Round Table: Environmental History”. doi:10.2307/2936586.

verification.note: English JAH text unread: the DOI resolves to the OUP page, which returned 403, and JSTOR returned a bot challenge. Crossref 10.2307/2936586 gives JAH 76:4, first page 1087; Crossref lists the round table's responses: Crosby 'An Enthusiastic Second' (1107), White 'Environmental History, Ecology, and Meaning' (1111), Merchant 'Gender and Environmental History' (1117), Cronon 'Modes of Prophecy and Production' (1122), Pyne 'Firestick History' (1132) and Worster's reply 'Seeing Beyond Culture' (1142). The whole article and notes were read in Portuguese translation ('Transformações da terra', Ambiente & Sociedade 5:2/6:1, 2002–03, pp. 23–44). The English wording quoted in this packet comes from Worster's reprint of the essay in The Wealth of Nature (1993, ch. 4; see pe131_worster_wealth_1993), checked by full-text search. JAH pages are given only where Isenberg 2013 cites them: p. 1091 for 'at once materialist and idealist' and 'the analysis of modes of production as ecological phenomena', both matching the 1993 wording. Worster's reply and the White, Cronon, Crosby and Pyne responses are unread.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period programmatic essay; English pages not seen.

new_sources.title: Donald Worster, The Wealth of Nature: Environmental History and the Ecological Imagination (New York: Oxford University Press, 1993).
new_sources.citation: Donald Worster, The Wealth of Nature: Environmental History and the Ecological Imagination (Oxford University Press, 1993), ch. 4, “Transformations of the Earth” (begins p. 45), and Notes, pp. 221–244.

verification.note: Internet Archive wealthofnatureen00wors (OUP 1993; Open Library OL1713212M, LCCN 92015360, ISBN 0195076249), lending-restricted; page images not seen. Checked by the archive's full-text search, which returns short snippets with running heads. Contents: ch. 3 'History as Natural History' p. 30; ch. 4 'Transformations of the Earth' p. 45; Notes p. 221; Index p. 245. Chapter 4 reprints the 1990 essay (the snippets match the Portuguese translation and Isenberg's JAH quotations); whether it was revised was not checked. Snippets used: 'There are three levels on which the new history proceeds, each drawing on a range'; 'at once materialist and idealist; they commonly maintain that the'; 'the second level of inquiry I mentioned'; 'that middle level, the analysis of modes of production as ecological phenomena, and particularly'; 'who has gained and who has lost power as modes of production have changed'; 'I submit that the single most important task for scholars in the history of modern agroecology is to trace what Karl Polanyi has called “the great transformation,”'; 'as sweeping and revolutionary a set of land-use changes as did the Neolithic revolution'; 'The reorganization of nature, not merely of society'. The index gives modes of production at 50, 52–63 and the great transformation at 56, 57–58. Chapter 4, note 5 (Annales passage) is on p. 226: the running head '226 Notes' precedes the end of chapter 3's notes (n. 32), and 'Notes 227' precedes chapter 4's n. 9, so chapter 4's notes 1–8 fall on p. 226. Its full wording is in NOTES.md.

new_sources.scope_note: Worster's 1993 reprint of the 1990 essay: source of the English wording quoted here.

new_sources.title: Carolyn Merchant, “Gender and Environmental History,” Journal of American History 76, no. 4 (March 1990): 1117–1121.
new_sources.citation: Carolyn Merchant, “Gender and Environmental History,” Journal of American History 76:4 (1990): 1117–1121, a response in the round table on Worster's “Transformations of the Earth”. doi:10.2307/2936589.

verification.note: Author-hosted JSTOR scan (stable 2936589), OCR'd locally at 300 dpi because the text layer is garbled; p. 1117 read closely, pp. 1120–1121 read. p. 1117: Worster's essay, 'while a rich and provocative approach to the field of environmental history, lacks a gender analysis. His conceptual levels of ecology (natural history), production (technology and its socioeconomic relations), and cognition (the mental realm of ideas, ethics, myths, and so on) are a significant framework for research and writing in this emerging field. His use of the mode-of-production concept in differing ecological and cultural contexts and his account of the changing history of ecological ideas in his major books have propelled environmental history to new levels of sophistication.' 'environmental history needs a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction, which interacts with the other three levels' (p. 1117). p. 1121: 'the shifts of power that Worster argues occurs in different environments are not only those between indigenous and invading cultures but also those between men and women.' The Merchant packet in this batch records the same article as pe131_merchant_jah_1990; the two records should be merged at release.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period round-table response: credits the three levels and adds gender and reproduction.

new_sources.title: William Cronon, “A Place for Stories: Nature, History, and Narrative,” Journal of American History 78, no. 4 (March 1992): 1347–1376.
new_sources.citation: William Cronon, “A Place for Stories: Nature, History, and Narrative,” Journal of American History 78:4 (1992): 1347–1376. doi:10.2307/2079346.

verification.note: Author-hosted PDF of the journal pages (running heads 'The Journal of American History March 1992'); text layer read for pp. 1347–1349 and 1363–1364. pp. 1347–1348: Bonnifield's and Worster's Dust Bowl books of 1979 'agreed on most of their facts, and yet their conclusions could hardly have been more different'; Cronon quotes Worster, Dust Bowl, p. 4: 'It came about because the culture was operating in precisely the way it was supposed to.... The Dust Bowl ... was the inevitable outcome of a culture that deliberately, self-consciously, set itself [the] task of dominating and exploiting the land for all it was worth.' p. 1363: Worster 'is with Webb the most powerful narrator'; the Plains are 'a paradigmatic case in a larger story that might be called “the rise and fall of capitalism”'; Cronon quotes Dust Bowl, p. 5: 'Capitalism, it is my contention, has been the decisive factor in this nation's use of nature'; 'the chief agent of the story is not “the pioneers” or “civilization” or “man”; it is capitalism'; the tale 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy that inverts the prophecy of progress found in earlier frontier narratives' (p. 1363). p. 1364: Worster 'acknowledges the prior presence of Indians in the region' but 'devotes only a few pages to them'. The Cronon packet in this batch records the same article as pe131_cronon_place_stories_1992; the two records should be merged at release.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period critique: Dust Bowl as a declensionist narrative with capitalism as its agent.

new_sources.title: Gregg R. Hennessey, review of Donald Worster, Rivers of Empire (1985), Journal of San Diego History 33, no. 4 (Fall 1987).
new_sources.citation: Gregg R. Hennessey, review of Worster, Rivers of Empire, Journal of San Diego History 33:4 (Fall 1987).

verification.note: Review read in full on the San Diego History Center page (online text, no print pagination). Quotes Rivers of Empire at pp. 4, 7, 130 and 206; Worster 'resurrects and revises the thesis of sometimes Marxist scholar Karl Wittfogel regarding ancient “hydraulic societies”'; 'the control of water, not land, has been the determining factor in the development of the arid West'; the book is 'a social historical analysis of irrigation in the arid West' and 'focuses primarily on the ideas behind irrigation'. Reservations: no bibliography; the dissenters Worster hopes will reform the system seem weak. A local historical society's review, not a historiographical assessment.
